definitions.definition: Brahman is the beginningless, endless Word-principle that appears as the world through its powers, time chief among them; all words finally denote it as Being (VP 1.1–4; 3.1–2).
The unmanifest sound arising from the supreme bindu, which is the consciousness of all beings, not the word or the meaning; it dwells as kuṇḍalinī and becomes the letters (ŚT 1.11–14).

relations.note: Brahman approached as the word (grammar, mantra) and as musical sound (saṅgīta)
the Kashmir Śaivas deny that the grammarians' paśyantī is the ultimate

definitions.definition: The consciousness of all beings unfolded as the world, bliss without a second, worshipped by nāda-worship through which Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara are worshipped (ŚR 1.3.1–2); without nāda there is no song, note or dance and the world is made of nāda (Bṛhaddeśī 16–18).

name: All cognition is permeated by the word (śabdānuviddha jñāna)

definitions.definition: No cognition occurs without the word; all knowledge shines as if pierced by it; awareness is word-natured (vāgrūpatā), which makes recognition possible, and speech is the consciousness of beings (VP 1.123–124 and following).

relations.note: the word-nature of awareness is traced back through madhyamā to paśyantī

notes: Denied by Buddhist logicians (non-conceptual perception is word-free) and by Śāntarakṣita's examination of the Word-brahman.

definitions.definition: Bhartṛhari names three — vaikharī (articulated), madhyamā (mental, sequential), paśyantī (undivided, sequence withdrawn) — and calls the Veda their supreme station (VP 1.142 with Vṛtti); Nāgeśa adds parā and locates the four in the root centre, navel, heart and throat.
Four levels — parā, paśyantī, madhyamā, vaikharī — as the stages by which śabda-brahman, dwelling as kuṇḍalinī, becomes the letters (ŚT 1.14).
Nāda rises from the knot of Brahmā through navel, heart, throat and head to the mouth and has five names by these places (ŚR 1.3.3–5; Bṛhaddeśī 23–25).

The word is a partless, sequence-less entity distinct from the sounds that manifest it; the sounds plant seeds in the intellect and with the last sound the sphoṭa is grasped; the sentence-sphoṭa is finally the only real one (VP 1.44, 1.73; Mahābhāṣya on P 1.1.70; VBhS sphoṭa-nirṇaya).

relations.note: the sphoṭa at its fullest is the sentence

definitions.definition: Letter-, word- and sentence-sphoṭa, each taken as individual or as universal (six), plus the partless word and partless sentence; the later grammarians hold only the sentence-sphoṭa real.

name: The sentence as the indivisible unit of meaning (akhaṇḍa-vākya)

definitions.definition: The sentence is partless; words and letters are abstractions (apoddhāra) from it; its meaning is grasped as pratibhā (VP 1.73; 2.1–2; 2.143).

name: Pratibhā: the flash of sentence meaning and instinct

definitions.definition: An indescribable intuition, self-evident to each, in which the sentence meaning is grasped; the guide of all action, even animals' instinct; sixfold by origin — nature, conduct, practice, yoga, unseen merit, and gift of the special ones (VP 2.143–152).

relations.note: same word; the grammarian's universal intuition and the poet's genius

name: What words denote: universal or substance

definitions.definition: Vājapyāyana: the universal; Vyāḍi: the individual substance; Patañjali accepts both; Bhartṛhari shows that both finally denote Being (sattā) / the Real, which is Brahman (Mahābhāṣya on P 1.2.64; VP 3.1–2).

name: Time as the power of the Word-Brahman

definitions.definition: Time is the independent power of Brahman by which sequence, birth and the other modifications appear; the 'wire-puller' of the world-machine (VP 1.3; 3.9).

name: Grammar as a path to liberation

definitions.definition: Grammar is nearest to Brahman, the highest austerity, the door to liberation and remedy for the impurities of speech, the first rung of the ladder and the straight royal road (VP 1.11–16); the refinement of words is the attainment of the supreme self (VP 1, verse uncertain); correct usage brings merit (Mahābhāṣya on 6.1.84).

name: Drama as the fifth Veda for all classes

definitions.definition: At the gods' request Brahmā made the Nāṭyaveda from the four Vedas — recitation, song, acting and rasa — because the Vedas may not be heard by śūdras; it is for all classes and shows the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.11–17, 1.107).

'Rasa arises from the union of determinants, consequents and transient states' (NŚ 6). Lollaṭa: intensification in the character; Śaṅkuka: inference in the actor; Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka: enjoyment through bhāvakatva and bhojakatva; Abhinavagupta: manifestation and relish in the spectator — the view adopted by Mammaṭa and Viśvanātha.

Forty-nine bhāvas: eight stable emotions (sthāyibhāva), thirty-three transient states (vyabhicāribhāva) and eight involuntary states (sāttvika); they 'bring into being' the poem's meaning; determinants (vibhāva) cause and consequents (anubhāva) express them (NŚ 6.17–22; 7.1–3).

relations.note: Rūpa Gosvāmī re-applies the same apparatus to love for Kṛṣṇa

definitions.definition: Śṛṅgāra (erotic), hāsya (comic), karuṇa (compassionate), raudra (furious), vīra (heroic), bhayānaka (terrible), bībhatsa (odious), adbhuta (marvellous) — eight in drama (NŚ 6.15); śānta (peace) as ninth in the NŚ's śānta passage, Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta and Mammaṭa ('lovely with nine rasas', KP 1.1); four are sources of the other four (NŚ 6.39–41). Others add preyas (Rudraṭa), vatsala (SD 3.251) or bhakti.

relations.note: Rūpa Gosvāmī's five primary and seven secondary devotional rasas re-arrange the nine

name: Śānta rasa: peace as an aesthetic experience akin to liberation

definitions.definition: The rasa leading to liberation, arising from knowledge of reality, dispassion and purity of mind, acted through yama, niyama and meditation; its stable emotion is calm (NŚ śānta passage; SD 3.245), dispassion (KP 4) or the self itself as knowledge of reality (Abhinavagupta); the natural state from which the other bhāvas arise and into which they dissolve; principal rasa of the Mahābhārata (DhĀ 4.5 vṛtti); denied a place in drama by Dhanañjaya.

relations.note: śānta is the rasa in which the relish of the self is thematized

notes: Advaita (Gauḍapāda, MK 3.45) calls tasting the bliss of samādhi (rasāsvāda) an obstacle — see obs:rasasvada; the poeticians' valuation is the opposite.

name: Aesthetic relish as consciousness at rest (brahmāsvāda-sahodara)

definitions.definition: Rasa is relished in a consciousness freed from personal limits and at rest in itself, a supermundane wonder; it is the 'twin' of tasting Brahman — undivided, self-luminous, bliss and consciousness, untouched by other objects (Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka as reported; Abhinavagupta; SD 3.2–3); for Jagannātha it is consciousness itself with its veil removed.

In aesthetic experience the determinants and emotions are freed from belonging to a particular person, time and place — neither 'mine' nor 'another's' — so that the spectator's limited self does not obstruct relish (Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka; Abhinavagupta).

Beyond denotation and indication, words and meanings suggest an implied sense — a fact, a figure or a rasa — which is the soul of poetry; rasa can only be suggested (DhĀ 1.1, 1.4, 1.13); the name comes from the grammarians' dhvani that manifests the sphoṭa.

relations.note: Ānandavardhana models dhvani on the grammarians' sounds manifesting the sphoṭa

name: The schools of poetics: what is the 'soul' of poetry?

definitions.definition: Figure (alaṅkāra: Bhāmaha, Daṇḍin), style (rīti: Vāmana), suggestion (dhvani: Ānandavardhana), oblique expression (vakrokti: Kuntaka), propriety (aucitya: Kṣemendra), rasa (Viśvanātha: 'a sentence whose soul is rasa'); inference (Mahimabhaṭṭa) as the critique of dhvani.

Fame, wealth, knowledge of conduct, removal of evil, immediate supreme bliss, and counsel in the manner of a beloved (KP 1.2); the four aims of life even for the dull, through poetry (SD 1.2); rest for the afflicted and instruction for all (NŚ 1.108–116).
The seed of poetry, together with skill and practice (KP 1.3); creative in the poet and appreciative in the connoisseur (Rājaśekhara).

Everything — song, instrument, dance, speech, the world — depends on nāda; it is named from breath (na) and fire (da), rises from the knot of Brahmā to the mouth in five forms, and is struck or unstruck (ŚR 1.2.1–3; 1.3.3–6; Bṛhaddeśī 16–25).
The second emanation from the supreme after Śakti; within the threefold bindu, the union of Śiva and Śakti (ŚT 1.7–9).

relations.note: the unstruck nāda of the yogins is the music treatises' anāhata

name: Struck and unstruck sound (āhata and anāhata nāda)

definitions.definition: Nāda is twofold (ŚR 1.2.3). The unstruck is worshipped by sages by the guru's path as an easy means to liberation but has no charm for people; the struck, made into music through śrutis and notes, delights the world and breaks worldly existence (ŚR 1.2.163–167).

name: Music as a path to liberation

definitions.definition: Struck nāda 'delights the world and breaks bondage' (ŚR 1.2.167); nāda-worship is worship of the three gods (ŚR 1.3.2); the knower of vīṇā, śrutis and tāla goes the way of liberation without effort, and the knower of song who fails in yoga becomes Rudra's attendant (YājS 3.115–116); for Tyāgarāja there is no liberation without devotion joined to knowledge of nāda.
Mārga: the 'sought-out' music fixed by Brahmā and Bharata, performed before Śiva for well-being; deśī: regional music sung at will that delights people (ŚR 1.1.22–23; Bṛhaddeśī 13).

name: Śruti, svara and grāma

definitions.definition: Twenty-two śrutis arising in channels at the heart; seven notes arising from them; two (or three) grāmas; demonstrated on two vīṇās (ŚR 1.3.7–25; NŚ 28).

members: 7 svaras (sa ri ga ma pa dha ni)

definitions.definition: A particular sound-form adorned with notes and melodic movement that colours the minds of people (Bṛhaddeśī 280–281); later classified by parent scales (mela) and by time, season and rasa.

name: The body's centres in the Saṅgītaratnākara

definitions.definition: Ten centres — ādhāra (4 petals), svādhiṣṭhāna (6), maṇipūra (10), anāhata (12), viśuddhi (16), lalanā (12), ājñā (3), manas (6), soma (16) and the thousand-petalled lotus — each petal giving a state of mind when the jīva rests there, and certain petals giving or destroying success in music (ŚR 1.2.120–144).

relations.note: partial: adds lalanā, manas and soma centres to the six-centre scheme

name: Śakti, nāda, bindu: the emanation of sound

definitions.definition: From the supreme Lord come Śakti, nāda and bindu; bindu divides into bindu (Śiva), bīja (Śakti) and nāda (their union); from them Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā and Vāmā, Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (will, knowledge, action); from the dividing bindu the unmanifest sound, śabda-brahman; from bindu-Śambhu Sadāśiva, Īśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu and Brahmā (ŚT 1.7–16).

Śabda-brahman, dwelling as kuṇḍalinī, manifests as the letters (ŚT 1.14); the fifty letters from a to kṣa are the Goddess's body and the matrix of all mantras, installed on the body in mātṛkā-nyāsa and used as a rosary of letters.

Mantras (male deity) and vidyās (female deity); male, female and neuter by their endings; fiery and lunar, awakening with the flow of breath in the right, left or both channels (ŚT 2.57–63); seed (bīja), compound (piṇḍa, kūṭa) and longer mantras.

name: Seed-syllables of the centres and elements

definitions.definition: The elements have the seeds laṃ (earth), vaṃ (water), raṃ (fire), yaṃ (air), haṃ (space) — placed in the root, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata and viśuddhi centres, with oṃ at the ājñā; the petals of the six centres carry the fifty letters (4+6+10+12+16+2); the seeds are used in the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and in meditation on the centres.
The Saṅgītaratnākara's throat centre carries on its petals the praṇava, udgītha, huṃ-phaṭ, vaṣaṭ, svadhā, svāhā, namaḥ, amṛta, the seven notes and poison (ŚR 1.2.129–130).

A mantra must be received from a qualified guru — pure, self-controlled, learned in the Āgamas and Veda, devoted to japa, calm, following yoga — by a qualified disciple who serves the guru and is tested one to four years according to class (ŚT 2.141–153); the mantra is kept secret (gopana is the tenth purification, ŚT 2.122); defective mantras must be purified (ŚT 2.64–123).

relations.note: the Śaiva initiation types into which mantra-dīkṣā fits

definitions.definition: The 'tāra' prefixed to mantras; its three letters are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra; its subtle phases beyond the three letters (bindu, ardhacandra, nirodhikā, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā, unmanā) are traversed in its meditative utterance.
The one word from which the Veda's knowledge springs (VP 1.9, low confidence).

relations.note: duplicate concept (U05) for the same syllable

name: The subtle phases of Oṃ's utterance

definitions.definition: After a, u, m the utterance of the praṇava passes through bindu, ardhacandra, nirodhikā, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā and unmanā, each subtler and shorter, sound dissolving into the soundless.
